subtopics.title: Unknown angles and sides in triangles
subtopics.exposition: A triangle is a three-sided polygon. Triangles can be classified according to their sides as equilateral, isosceles or scalene. Triangles can also be classified according to their angles as acute-angled, obtuse-angled or right-angled. A scalene triangle has all sides and angles different. An isosceles triangle has two sides equal in length. An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal in length and all three angles equal. An acute triangle has each of its three interior angles less than 90°. An obtuse triangle has one interior angle greater than 90°. A right-angled triangle has one interior angle equal to 90°. Properties from the classification by sides and by angles can be combined in one triangle; for example, an obtuse isosceles triangle and a right-angled isosceles triangle are possible. In an isosceles triangle, the angles opposite the equal sides are also equal. The angles in a triangle add up to 180°. Theorem of Pythagoras: if △ABC is right-angled with B̂ = 90°, then b² = a² + c². Converse of the theorem of Pythagoras: if b² = a² + c², then △ABC is right-angled with B̂ = 90°. In the interior-angles Investigation, the three angles cut from a triangle are placed along a ruler (a straight line), with the hint to think about the sum of angles on a straight line. To find an unknown angle in a triangle, write the sum of the three angles equal to 180° with the reason (sum of angles in a triangle), substitute the known angles and solve; for example 90° + 35° + Ê = 180°, so Ê = 55°. To find an unknown side of a right-angled triangle, write the theorem of Pythagoras for that triangle (CE² = DE² + CD²), substitute the known lengths (5² = 3² + x²) and solve (x² = 16, so x = 4). To find an unknown angle in the second triangle, apply the sum of angles in a triangle again: B̂ + Â + ŷ = 180°, so 90° + 55° + ŷ = 180° and ŷ = 35°. The notation △ABC refers to a triangle with vertices labelled A, B and C. In worked solutions, each statement is followed by its reason in brackets, such as (given), (proved), (sum of angles in a triangle), (Pythagoras) or (AAS).

subtopics.title: Congruent triangles
subtopics.exposition: Two triangles are congruent if one fits exactly over the other. Congruent triangles have equal corresponding angles and sides. RHS (also written 90° HS: 90°, hypotenuse, side): if the hypotenuse and one side of a right-angled triangle are equal to the hypotenuse and the corresponding side of another right-angled triangle, then the two triangles are congruent. SSS (side, side, side): if three sides of a triangle are equal in length to the corresponding sides of another triangle, then the two triangles are congruent. SAS (also written S∠S: side, angle, side): if two sides and the included angle of a triangle are equal to the corresponding two sides and included angle of another triangle, then the two triangles are congruent. AAS (also written ∠∠S: angle, angle, side): if one side and two angles of a triangle are equal to the corresponding one side and two angles of another triangle, then the two triangles are congruent. Writing △ABC ≡ △DEF indicates that Â = D̂, B̂ = Ê, Ĉ = F̂, AB = DE, AC = DF and BC = EF; the letters are matched in order. To determine whether two triangles are congruent, it is not necessary to check every side and every angle. To determine whether two triangles are congruent, name the two triangles, list pairs of equal angles and sides each with its reason (given or proved), and conclude the congruence with the rule used, here AAS, writing △CDE ≡ △CBA in corresponding order. Once the triangles are proved congruent, use the congruence to equate corresponding sides: since △CDE ≡ △CBA, CE = CA, so z = 5. Congruency is indicated using the symbol ≡. The symbol ≅ may also be used to show that two triangles are congruent; it is the internationally recognised symbol for congruency.

subtopics.title: Similar triangles
subtopics.exposition: Two triangles are similar if one triangle is a scaled version of the other. Similar triangles have the same shape but different scales. Similar triangles have corresponding angles equal in measure and the ratios of their corresponding sides in proportion. Congruent triangles are similar triangles, but not all similar triangles are congruent. AAA (angle, angle, angle): if all three pairs of corresponding angles of two triangles are equal, then the triangles are similar. SSS (side, side, side): if all three pairs of corresponding sides of two triangles are in proportion, then the triangles are similar. To show similarity by AAA, state the three pairs of equal corresponding angles (Â = D̂, B̂ = Ê, Ĉ = F̂) and conclude △ABC ||| △DEF. To show similarity by SSS, show that MN/RS = ML/RT = NL/ST, and conclude △MNL ||| △RST. Similarity of two triangles is indicated using the symbol |||. The symbol ∼ may also be used to show that two triangles are similar; it is the internationally recognised symbol for similarity.

The angles in a triangle add up to 180°.
Two triangles are congruent if one fits exactly over the other.
Congruent triangles have equal corresponding angles and sides.
To determine whether two triangles are congruent, it is not necessary to check every side and every angle.

RHS (also written 90° HS: 90°, hypotenuse, side): if the hypotenuse and one side of a right-angled triangle are equal to the hypotenuse and the corresponding side of another right-angled triangle, then the two triangles are congruent.
SSS (side, side, side): if three sides of a triangle are equal in length to the corresponding sides of another triangle, then the two triangles are congruent.

SAS (also written S∠S: side, angle, side): if two sides and the included angle of a triangle are equal to the corresponding two sides and included angle of another triangle, then the two triangles are congruent.
AAS (also written ∠∠S: angle, angle, side): if one side and two angles of a triangle are equal to the corresponding one side and two angles of another triangle, then the two triangles are congruent.
The order of letters when labelling congruent triangles is very important.
Writing △ABC ≡ △DEF indicates that Â = D̂, B̂ = Ê, Ĉ = F̂, AB = DE, AC = DF and BC = EF; the letters are matched in order.
The symbol ≅ may also be used to show that two triangles are congruent; it is the internationally recognised symbol for congruency.
Two triangles are similar if one triangle is a scaled version of the other.
Similar triangles have corresponding angles equal in measure and the ratios of their corresponding sides in proportion.
Similar triangles have the same shape but different scales.
Congruent triangles are similar triangles, but not all similar triangles are congruent.
Similarity of two triangles is indicated using the symbol |||.
AAA (angle, angle, angle): if all three pairs of corresponding angles of two triangles are equal, then the triangles are similar.
To show similarity by AAA, state the three pairs of equal corresponding angles (Â = D̂, B̂ = Ê, Ĉ = F̂) and conclude △ABC ||| △DEF.
SSS (side, side, side): if all three pairs of corresponding sides of two triangles are in proportion, then the triangles are similar.
To show similarity by SSS, show that MN/RS = ML/RT = NL/ST, and conclude △MNL ||| △RST.
The order of letters for similar triangles is very important; similar triangles must always be labelled in corresponding order.
△MNL ||| △RST is correct, but △MNL ||| △RTS is incorrect.
The symbol ∼ may also be used to show that two triangles are similar; it is the internationally recognised symbol for similarity.
